meta.name: ASTRA PULSE - NASA-sourced predictor/reference file
meta.purpose: Compact rule/reference library for astronaut health monitoring. Indicators and their reference data are preserved from v2.

evidence_levels.NASA_supported_mechanism: NASA supports the mechanism; the exact combined rule may not be validated.
evidence_levels.plausible_combined_indicator: Useful monitoring pattern, but not a validated threshold or diagnosis.

meta.baseline_note: Personal-baseline comparisons are app-level logic, not NASA clinical limits. Compare measurements from the same mission phase and relevant context.
meta.safety_note: Decision support only, not diagnosis or treatment. Missing data are not normal. Escalate concerning symptoms or results to mission medical staff/flight surgeon. Countermeasures must follow approved mission protocols.
meta.rule_note: Compound rules are monitoring flags. Evaluate only when all required measurements are available for the relevant time window and mission phase.
meta.description: Compact ASTRA PULSE 20-indicator library with per-indicator NASA/spaceflight source traceability and all 6 compound predictions preserved.

bibliography_audit.method: Web verification against NASA NTRS, official NASA OCHMO pages/PDFs, PubMed/PMC and journal publisher records. Bibliographic existence and claim support assessed separately. Added a direct review of NASA OCHMO-MTB-009 (Circadian Desynchrony, 4 Mar 2026) to replace the generic sleep-countermeasure placeholder.

status_definitions.verified: Bibliographic identity and core metadata confirmed against a primary or authoritative record.
status_definitions.corrected: Source exists but one or more citation fields were wrong or materially incomplete; citation corrected.
status_definitions.partially_verified: A source or URL exists, but metadata or claimed support remains incomplete/secondary.
status_definitions.unverified_placeholder: Not a complete, traceable bibliographic source.

bibliography_audit.important_limit: A verified bibliography does not automatically validate every used_for claim, threshold, or indicator. Review each bibliography_audit_note and retain cohort/mission context; unresolved claims are explicitly flagged.

co2_ochmo.bibliography_audit_note: Official NASA OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide, Revision D, dated 10-Mar-2026, was located. The cited one-hour and seven-day averaging windows must remain attached to their respective limits; do not apply them to instantaneous sensor values.

moore_2014.citation: Moore AD Jr, Downs ME, Lee SMC, Feiveson AH, Knudsen P, Evetts SN, Ploutz-Snyder L. Peak Oxygen Uptake during and after Long-duration Space Flight. NASA NTRS 20140003748; JSC-CN-29966. 2014.

downs_2014.citation: Downs ME, Buxton R, Moore A, Ploutz-Snyder R, Ploutz-Snyder L. Contributions of astronauts' aerobic exercise intensity and time on change in VO2peak during spaceflight. NASA abstract NTRS 20140003747.

nasa_circadian_brief_2026.used_for: NASA description of circadian desynchrony and associations with sleep disruption, inattention, slowed reaction time, and impaired decision-making.
nasa_circadian_brief_2026.bibliography_audit_note: Official NASA PDF confirms OCHMO-MTB-009, Circadian Desynchrony, NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer, dated 4-Mar-2026. The JSON incorrectly labels it “NASA-STD-3001 Medical Technical Brief” in a way that could imply it is itself a standard; NASA states the brief is derived from NASA-STD-3001 and medical operations, for reference only.

sleep_countermeasure_guidance.citation: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO). Circadian Desynchrony. NASA-STD-3001 Medical Technical Brief OCHMO-MTB-009. 4 March 2026.
sleep_countermeasure_guidance.nasa_link: NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief; derived from NASA-STD-3001 and NASA medical operations.
sleep_countermeasure_guidance.used_for: NASA-described sleep/fatigue management education and assessment; sleep-shift scheduling consultation; sleep hygiene and sleep-environment practices (cool, dark, quiet sleep space); timed light-exposure practices; avoiding vigorous exercise close to bedtime. Supports operational context and countermeasure categories, not a numeric alert threshold or autonomous treatment recommendation.
sleep_countermeasure_guidance.bibliography_audit_note: Replaced the generic untraceable placeholder with the official NASA OCHMO Medical Technical Brief OCHMO-MTB-009, Circadian Desynchrony, dated 4 March 2026. The PDF identifies the NASA-STD-3001 medical technical brief and describes sleep/fatigue education, assessment, sleep-shift scheduling consultation, sleep hygiene, timed light exposure, and avoiding vigorous exercise within two hours of sleep (PDF pp. 3–4). It explicitly states that it is a reference brief and not direct medical-care guidance. It supports the listed countermeasure context only; it does not validate ASTRA PULSE compound-rule thresholds or authorize medication/countermeasure prescriptions.

nasa_rst_iss_technical_publication.bibliography_audit_note: Official NASA technical publication PDF confirms title Psychomotor Vigilance Self Test on the International Space Station (Reaction Self Test). sleep_hours.label: Sleep duration

cited_rules.message: Six hours or less was associated with slower psychomotor response speed and higher stress in a longitudinal study of 24 ISS astronauts. NASA schedules an 8.5-hour sleep opportunity; this is not the same as actual sleep duration.
cited_rules.action: Protect the next scheduled sleep opportunity; review schedule, light exposure and sleep environment. Avoid vigorous exercise close to bedtime. Refer persistent performance or mood changes to the mission medical team.

cited_rules.message: Between 6 and 7 hours: above the <=6-hour band associated with slower psychomotor response in one ISS study, but below NASA's scheduled 8.5-hour sleep opportunity. This is not a declaration of adequate sleep.
Seven hours or more. Continue to assess sleep quality, circadian timing and individual baseline; NASA's scheduled sleep opportunity is 8.5 hours.

window_rules.message: Your 7-day average sleep is 6 h or less, the level associated with measurable psychomotor slowing and higher stress in ISS astronauts (sleep debt is accumulating).
window_rules.action: Treat this as accumulated sleep debt: schedule recovery sleep and tell the crew surgeon/clinician if performance or mood is affected.

sleep_hours.measurement_context: Daily sleep episode; distinguish actual sleep from scheduled sleep opportunity.

scheduled_sleep_opportunity_reference.note: Schedule allocation, not an actual-sleep average, universal requirement for this rule engine, or diagnostic threshold.

astronaut_cohorts.finding: Mean sleep about 5.96 h on Shuttle and 6.09 h on ISS in the studied cohorts.

astronaut_cohorts.population: 24 astronauts on six-month ISS missions; 2,856 Reaction SelfTest assessments
astronaut_cohorts.finding: Reported sleep was approximately 6.5 h; <=6 h was associated with slower psychomotor response speed and higher stress.

astronaut_cohorts.population: 2,137 in-flight nights in the reported dataset
astronaut_cohorts.finding: Mean in-flight sleep about 7.33 +/- 1.16 h in the reported analysis; estimates differ across cohorts and methods.

research_summary.interpretation: Do not merge these cohort estimates into one universal astronaut sleep norm. Differences in cohorts, methods, schedule and mission periods matter.

sleep_hours.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut studies report sleep duration and associations with performance. The <=6 h rule is a study-associated watch level, not a universal clinical sleep threshold; the 8.5 h value is scheduled sleep opportunity, not actual sleep.

sleep_efficiency_pct.label: Sleep efficiency

phase_notes.inflight: Reference is a single NASA slide table of unclear sample size; treat z-scores as indicative only.

sleep_efficiency_pct.measurement_context: Nightly sleep estimate from actigraphy or validated sleep measurement; denominator is time in bed / sleep opportunity as defined by the instrument.
sleep_efficiency_pct.provisional_note: 89% (SD 3) is an example from a NASA slide table with unclear sample size. Treat as descriptive only, not an operational or clinical limit.
sleep_efficiency_pct.reference_audit_note: A NASA actigraphy presentation provides an example value, but sample-size/context limitations mean it is descriptive only, not a validated operational or clinical threshold.

circadian_misaligned.label: Circadian misalignment flag

cited_rules.message: Circadian disruption (e.g. shifted sleep periods) is one of the fatigue drivers the NASA/TRISH Reaction Self Test was built to detect; the standard ISS sleep window is about 21:30-06:00.
cited_rules.action: Re-anchor sleep timing gradually and use light timing; expect slower reaction time for a few days.

window_rules.message: Misalignment on 3 or more of the last 5 days is an app-level persistence rule to distinguish a recurring schedule shift from a one-off. This 3-of-5 threshold is not a NASA clinical limit.
window_rules.action: Review work/rest schedule and appropriately timed light exposure with mission fatigue-management staff.

circadian_misaligned.measurement_context: Daily flag derived from sleep timing relative to the crew member's planned schedule / circadian plan; retain sleep start/end timestamps where possible.

items: Maintain a consistent sleep/wake schedule where mission operations permit.
Use appropriately timed bright light after waking and reduce bright/blue-enriched light before planned sleep.
Keep the sleep environment dark, quiet and appropriately cool.
Avoid vigorous exercise close to bedtime; exercise remains an essential countermeasure and should be scheduled appropriately.
Review persistent shifts with mission fatigue-management staff.
countermeasure_summary.caution: Timing must be adapted to the crew schedule and approved operational guidance.

circadian_misaligned.reference_audit_note: NASA-supported fatigue monitoring considers sleep timing and circadian disruption. The app persistence rule is an implementation choice, not a NASA clinical cutoff.

resting_hr_bpm.label: Resting heart rate
resting_hr_bpm.context_action: Sit or lie down, hydrate, and get a clinician/flight surgeon to review if you feel light-headed on standing. (General advice; EDOMP notes orthostatic intolerance usually resolves in 1-2 days.)

phase_notes.inflight: No numeric in-flight norm was extracted. NASA found heart rate and diastolic pressure were lower in flight than preflight (Fritsch-Yelle 1996, 12 Shuttle astronauts), so your own preflight / in-flight baseline is the better yardstick; a rise above it is more notable than a fall.
phase_notes.postflight: NASA measured L+7 to L+10 only; for days 1-6 there is no numeric reference. EDOMP found cardiovascular changes resolved within 7 days of landing.

resting_hr_bpm.measurement_context: Resting measurement with posture, time of day and mission phase recorded.
resting_hr_bpm.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut cohorts provide phase- and posture-specific heart-rate observations. Use the matching mission phase, posture, and personal baseline; do not apply a single value to every crew member.

systolic_mmHg.context_action: Sit or lie down, hydrate, and get a clinician/flight surgeon to review if you feel light-headed on standing. (General advice; EDOMP notes orthostatic intolerance usually resolves in 1-2 days.)

phase_notes.inflight: No numeric in-flight norm was extracted. NASA found heart rate and diastolic pressure were lower in flight than preflight (Fritsch-Yelle 1996, 12 Shuttle astronauts), so your own preflight / in-flight baseline is the better yardstick; a rise above it is more notable than a fall.
phase_notes.postflight: NASA measured L+7 to L+10 only; for days 1-6 there is no numeric reference. EDOMP found cardiovascular changes resolved within 7 days of landing.

systolic_mmHg.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut studies provide phase- and posture-specific cohort values, not universal clinical limits for individual crew members.

diastolic_mmHg.context_action: Sit or lie down, hydrate, and get a clinician/flight surgeon to review if you feel light-headed on standing. (General advice; EDOMP notes orthostatic intolerance usually resolves in 1-2 days.)

phase_notes.inflight: No numeric in-flight norm was extracted. NASA found heart rate and diastolic pressure were lower in flight than preflight (Fritsch-Yelle 1996, 12 Shuttle astronauts), so your own preflight / in-flight baseline is the better yardstick; a rise above it is more notable than a fall.
phase_notes.postflight: NASA measured L+7 to L+10 only; for days 1-6 there is no numeric reference. EDOMP found cardiovascular changes resolved within 7 days of landing.

diastolic_mmHg.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut studies provide phase- and posture-specific cohort values, not universal clinical limits for individual crew members.

stroke_volume_ml.label: Stroke volume
stroke_volume_ml.reference_info: EDOMP Table 1-6 (mean+/-SE): supine preflight 83+/-4 mL (non-presyncopal, n=21) and 86+/-5 mL (presyncopal, n=8); landing day supine 77+/-5 and 78+/-4 mL; landing-day standing 32+/-9 and 28+/-2 mL. Table 1-2: stroke-volume INDEX fell 17% supine on landing day (38.5 -> 32.1 mL/m2). These are group means, so no automatic z-score is made.

phase_notes.landing_day: Expect roughly a 17% fall in supine stroke volume index vs your own preflight value (EDOMP, 32 astronauts); heart rate rises to compensate.
phase_notes.inflight: NASA did not provide a numeric in-flight stroke volume norm in the sources used; compare with your own baseline.

stroke_volume_ml.reference_audit_note: NASA/spaceflight studies report stroke-volume changes, but results vary by mission phase, posture, measurement method, and cohort. No single universal astronaut reference range is assigned.

vo2_pct_baseline.label: VO2 as % of preflight baseline

cited_rules.message: At or above the lower 95% bound of the mean early-flight VO2peak (about 83% of preflight, 95% CI 78-87%) measured in ISS astronauts.
Below the mean early-flight range but within the +5% to -30% individual spread NASA reported.
cited_rules.action: Check in-flight exercise time and intensity; both independently predicted VO2peak change (Downs 2014).

cited_rules.message: More than the 30% maximum decline in the NASA ISS series.
cited_rules.action: Review exercise countermeasure compliance and equipment with the exercise physiologist / flight surgeon.

cited_rules.message: Thirty or more days after landing VO2peak was within 2% of preflight (95% CI -6% to +3%); yours is below that.

phase_notes.inflight: VO2peak fell ~17% early in flight, then rose slowly but never fully returned to preflight (Moore 2014). Longer missions and older age were associated with larger loss (npj Microgravity 2023).
phase_notes.postflight: Expected about 15% below preflight on R+1 and back to within ~2% by R+30.

vo2_pct_baseline.measurement_context: Scheduled maximal or peak exercise test; record protocol, modality, test date, mission phase and preflight reference.
vo2_pct_baseline.additional_monitoring_note: A value near 80% of preflight represents an approximately 20% decline and is worth reviewing in context. Do not treat 80% as a diagnosis or universal clinical threshold.
vo2_pct_baseline.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut studies quantify changes from preflight VO2peak and exercise associations. Cohort changes are not individual diagnostic thresholds; compare with the crew member’s own preflight baseline and test protocol.

aerobic_min.label: Aerobic exercise minutes

phase_notes.inflight: NASA found exercise time and intensity independently affect VO2peak change, with minimum values needed to maintain it (Downs 2014), but no numeric minutes target was extracted, so only your own 7-day baseline is checked.

aerobic_min.measurement_context: Daily sum of aerobic exercise minutes; preserve session-level duration, modality and intensity when available.

research_summary.finding: Exercise time and intensity independently contributed to VO2peak change in a study of 11 astronauts with 110 observations.
research_summary.study_specific_recommendation: The 2014 study discussed at least 160 min/week of aerobic exercise at average intensity above 75% of peak HR, with additional time above 90%. This is not a universal current NASA prescription and must not be used as an autonomous target.

aerobic_min.reference_audit_note: NASA describes ISS aerobic exercise practices and study-specific dose/intensity associations. The programme is mission- and person-specific; do not turn study recommendations or cohort averages into a universal target.

spo2_pct.label: Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2)

inflight|any.label: In-flight SpO2 at inspired O2 127 mmHg (8 Shuttle astronauts)

uncited_defaults.message: Below 90% is generally treated as significant hypoxaemia.

spo2_pct.reference_audit_note: Oxygen saturation is included in NASA periodic health monitoring and has been studied under hypoxia/microgravity conditions. No universal astronaut-specific SpO2 alert threshold is assigned here.

fatigue_0_100.label: Fatigue rating
fatigue_0_100.no_nasa_reference: No NASA numeric cut-off exists for this 0-100 scale; only the personal 7-day baseline is applied.

late_mission_note.message: Self-rated stress rose in the 3rd and 4th quarters of 6-month ISS missions (Dinges 2014), so a late-mission rise in fatigue is common but still worth acting on.

fatigue_0_100.measurement_context: Self-reported rating; record scale wording, anchors and time of day consistently.
fatigue_0_100.reference_audit_note: NASA Reaction Self Test studies collect subjective fatigue-related ratings, but this 0-100 app scale has no NASA cut-off. Use the same scale consistently and compare with personal baseline.

pvt_lapses.label: PVT lapses
pvt_lapses.no_nasa_reference: Lapse = reaction >=355 ms on the 3-min PVT-B (NASA's ISS Reaction Self Test) or >=500 ms on the standard PVT (Basner 2011). No NASA absolute cut-off for lapse counts was found, so your own baseline is used.
pvt_lapses.measurement_context: Per standardised vigilance test; store test duration and protocol with every result.
pvt_lapses.interpretation_note: Do not compare lapse counts across different PVT protocols or test durations. No NASA absolute lapse-count alert threshold was identified; use within-person trend.
pvt_lapses.reference_audit_note: The lapse definition depends on test version (355 ms for 3-minute PVT-B; 500 ms for standard PVT). NASA does not establish a universal count-of-lapses alert threshold; compare counts using the same protocol and personal baseline.

poms_score.label: POMS mood score (weekly)
poms_score.no_nasa_reference: No NASA numeric POMS norm was found; checked only against your own previous weekly scores (higher = more mood disturbance is assumed; reverse if your scoring differs).

late_mission_note.message: Stress ratings rose in the second half of 6-month ISS missions (Dinges 2014).

poms_score.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut research includes subjective mood/stress and fatigue assessments, but no directly applicable NASA POMS numeric reference range was verified for this field. Retain the exact questionnaire/version and scoring direction; use personal trends.

resistance_min.label: Resistance exercise minutes
resistance_min.measurement_context: Per session, summed daily; distinguish completed exercise from scheduled time.
resistance_min.no_nasa_reference: No universal numeric resistance-minutes threshold is assigned here. Compare with the astronaut's prescribed programme and personal trend.
resistance_min.reference_audit_note: NASA describes ISS resistive exercise practices, including a typical 30-60 minute session range in the brief. This is programme guidance, not a universal prescription; compare with the individual mission plan.

headache_flag.label: Headache symptom flag
headache_flag.measurement_context: Self-reported symptom with timestamp and severity if available.
headache_flag.no_nasa_reference: No single headache flag is diagnostic; interpret with CO2 exposure and other symptoms.
headache_flag.reference_audit_note: NASA reports headache associations with elevated CO2 exposure, but a headache flag alone has no NASA diagnostic threshold. Interpret alongside time-averaged CO2 and other symptoms.

dizziness_standing_flag.label: Dizziness on standing flag
dizziness_standing_flag.measurement_context: Self-reported symptom recorded during or immediately after a posture transition.
dizziness_standing_flag.no_nasa_reference: Symptom flag only; interpret with posture-specific HR/BP and mission phase.
dizziness_standing_flag.reference_audit_note: NASA astronaut studies document orthostatic cardiovascular changes and symptoms. The flag is not diagnostic; interpret with posture-specific HR/BP, mission phase, and clinical protocol.

compound_rules.title: Sleep-related neurobehavioral performance decline
compound_rules.logic: ALL of sleep_hours in watch/act AND ANY of pvt_lapses baseline_bad, fatigue_0_100 baseline_bad.
compound_rules.possible_concern: Neurobehavioral performance impairment associated with sleep restriction
compound_rules.message: Short sleep combined with a worse-than-baseline vigilance or fatigue measure is consistent with the sleep-related performance pattern observed in ISS astronauts. This is not a diagnosis.
compound_rules.action: Flag for mission fatigue/performance review; do not autonomously clear or ground a crew member.
compound_rules.threshold_note: The <=6 h sleep band is source-supported; baseline-deviation checks for PVT lapse count and fatigue are app-level comparisons.

compound_rules.title: Persistent sleep disruption with circadian misalignment
compound_rules.logic: ALL of circadian_misaligned true on >=3 of 5 days AND (sleep_hours below personal baseline OR pvt_lapses baseline_bad OR fatigue_0_100 baseline_bad).
compound_rules.possible_concern: Persistent circadian desynchrony with sleep or performance disruption
compound_rules.message: Repeated sleep-timing misalignment together with reduced sleep or deteriorating performance warrants a schedule and fatigue-management review. The 3-of-5-day persistence setting is an app rule, not a NASA medical threshold.
compound_rules.action: Watch for persistence and performance effects; escalate if significant or worsening.
compound_rules.threshold_note: The 3-of-5-day rule is an implementation choice. No universal circadian misalignment threshold is claimed.

compound_rules.title: Reduced exercise participation with declining aerobic capacity
compound_rules.logic: ALL of vo2_pct_baseline below personal/preflight trend AND (aerobic_min below personal trend OR resistance_min below personal trend).
compound_rules.message: A decline in VO2peak together with reduced completion of the prescribed exercise programme is consistent with an aerobic deconditioning risk pattern. Exercise minutes alone do not establish deconditioning.
compound_rules.action: Exercise-programme review; do not generate a new exercise prescription automatically.
compound_rules.threshold_note: Use mission-specific prescription and within-person VO2peak trend. Do not treat the study-specific 160 min/week suggestion as a universal target.

compound_rules.title: Postflight orthostatic intolerance risk pattern
compound_rules.logic: ALL of postflight/landing phase AND dizziness_standing_flag AND abnormal posture-specific HR/BP or reduced stroke_volume_ml relative to personal preflight reference.
compound_rules.possible_concern: Orthostatic intolerance / presyncope risk during return to gravity
compound_rules.message: Standing-related dizziness together with a posture-specific cardiovascular change after landing requires medical review. EDOMP findings are cohort averages from Shuttle astronauts, not diagnostic cut-offs.
compound_rules.threshold_note: Require posture, mission phase and measurement timing. Do not use the group mean HR/BP values as universal thresholds.

compound_rules.title: Cabin CO2-associated symptom pattern
compound_rules.logic: ALL of cabin_co2_mmHg elevated over the applicable averaging window AND (headache_flag OR sleep_hours baseline_bad OR sleep_efficiency_pct baseline_bad).
compound_rules.possible_concern: Cabin CO2 may be contributing to headache or sleep symptoms
compound_rules.message: Elevated cabin CO2 together with headache or sleep disruption warrants an environmental review. Symptoms can have multiple causes and are not proof of CO2 causation.
compound_rules.threshold_note: NASA-STD-3001 cited one-hour average ppCO2 limit is 3 mmHg; NASA material also discusses a seven-day average below 2.5 mmHg. Do not compare a single instantaneous reading to a time-averaged standard.

exercise_monitoring.purpose: Monitor prescribed exercise participation, training intensity and physiological outcomes without turning population averages into personal exercise prescriptions.

equipment_context.name: ARED
equipment_context.purpose: Resistance exercise to provide muscular and skeletal loading.

equipment_context.name: T2 treadmill
equipment_context.purpose: Walking/running with harness and bungee loading.

programme_context.typical_iss_description: Long-duration ISS programmes combine aerobic and resistance exercise on most days. NASA overview material describes roughly 600 minutes/week total exercise in a dataset; this is not 600 minutes of aerobic exercise and is not an individual prescription.
programme_context.caution: Actual exercise plan, intensity zones and recovery schedule must come from mission medical/exercise staff.

exercise_monitoring.data_frequency: Session-level exercise data; daily and 7-day aggregates for participation; VO2peak only at scheduled fitness tests.

severity_0_3.label: Motion sickness severity (0-3)

cited_rules.message: Mild: transient symptoms, no operational impact, usually resolve in 36-48 h (NASA classification).
cited_rules.action: Move slowly, limit abrupt head movements, hydrate.

cited_rules.message: Mild symptoms are still present after the first ~72 h, longer than the 30-48 h in which space sickness usually resolves.
cited_rules.action: Limit abrupt head movements, hydrate and rest; if symptoms are moderate or beyond ~72 h, contact the flight surgeon / a clinician (NASA treated SMS with antiemetics such as promethazine in flight).

cited_rules.message: Moderate: several persistent symptoms with minimal operational impact; NASA expects resolution within ~72 h.
cited_rules.action: Limit abrupt head movements, hydrate and rest; if symptoms are moderate or beyond ~72 h, contact the flight surgeon / a clinician (NASA treated SMS with antiemetics such as promethazine in flight).

cited_rules.message: Moderate symptoms beyond ~72 h are outside the normal NASA time course.
cited_rules.action: Limit abrupt head movements, hydrate and rest; if symptoms are moderate or beyond ~72 h, contact the flight surgeon / a clinician (NASA treated SMS with antiemetics such as promethazine in flight).

cited_rules.message: Severe: persistent symptoms with significant performance decrement; may persist beyond 72 h (NASA classification). Untreated SMS can cause dehydration and difficulty completing tasks.
cited_rules.action: Limit abrupt head movements, hydrate and rest; if symptoms are moderate or beyond ~72 h, contact the flight surgeon / a clinician (NASA treated SMS with antiemetics such as promethazine in flight).

phase_notes.all: Typical NASA time course: onset ~1 h after orbital insertion, peak within 24-48 h, usually resolved by 30-48 h, up to 72 h.

severity_0_3.reference_audit_note: NASA space-motion-sickness classification sources support the severity scale. It is a symptom-severity classification, not a standalone diagnosis.

context_notes.message: First flight: 67% of 85 first-time Shuttle crew had some space motion sickness (30% mild, 24% moderate, 13% severe); NASA states 60-80% of space travellers are affected in the first 2-3 days.
Prior susceptibility is informative: in NASA Shuttle data, susceptibility on a first flight predicted susceptibility on the second in 77% of cases (secondary source).
No motion sickness was reported on the 1/6 g lunar surface in Apollo accounts (secondary source); symptoms are tied to transitions between gravity levels.
No NASA-cited effect of sex or age on space motion sickness was found in the sources reviewed, so these are not used as predictors.

core_temp_rest_c.label: Resting core temperature

text.none: Resting core temperature in ISS crew rose about 1.01 C above their own baseline, gradually over ~2.5 months. Yours is {delta:+.2f} C vs your preflight mean: no elevation yet.
text.typical: Resting core temperature is {delta:+.2f} C vs your preflight mean; ISS crew showed an average rise of about +1.01 C over ~2.5 months (Stahn 2017), so this is in the expected direction.
text.above: Resting core temperature is {delta:+.2f} C vs your preflight mean, above the average +1.01 C rise in ISS crew. NASA-coauthored data give the mean only here, so judge it with your 7-day baseline and symptoms.

uncited_defaults.message: 38.0 C or higher is the usual terrestrial fever threshold.

phase_notes.inflight: Core temperature rises gradually in flight (+1.01 C at rest, associated with higher IL-1ra), so the preflight baseline matters more than the textbook 37 C.

core_temp_rest_c.reference_audit_note: Stahn et al. report a gradual average resting core-temperature increase during long-duration spaceflight. The cohort change is not a fever definition or individual clinical limit; compare with preflight baseline and time of day.

core_temp_exercise_peak_c.label: Exercise peak core temperature

cited_rules.message: Exercise core temperature exceeded 40 C in some ISS astronauts (Stahn 2017, per secondary summary); NASA has not published this as a limit, but it is high.
cited_rules.action: Stop or lower exercise intensity, cool down, hydrate; report to the flight surgeon / a clinician if you feel unwell.

core_temp_exercise_peak_c.reference_audit_note: NASA-associated research reports exercise core-temperature observations, but the 40 C value in the existing rule is not a NASA-published operational or diagnostic limit.

cabin_co2_mmHg.label: Cabin CO2

cited_rules.message: At or above the 3 mmHg limit NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev D sets for the 1-hour average ppCO2 (a daily mean above it means some hours were higher). NASA lists chronic cough, poor sleep, blurred vision and frontal headaches around 3.5 mmHg.
cited_rules.action: Improve ventilation / check CO2 removal, reduce exertion, report headache or other symptoms to the flight surgeon or a clinician.

cited_rules.message: Below the 3 mmHg limit but in the range where ISS crew started reporting CO2-related symptoms (from 2.3 mmHg).
cited_rules.action: Watch for headache, poor sleep or 'mental viscosity'; check ventilation around your sleep and work area.

cited_rules.message: Below the level at which ISS crew began reporting CO2 symptoms.

window_rules.message: 7-day mean CO2 is at or above 2.5 mmHg; NASA reports the 7-day average must stay below 2.5 mmHg to keep headache incidence under 1%.
window_rules.action: Look for a sustained ventilation problem rather than a single bad day.

cabin_co2_mmHg.reference_audit_note: NASA-STD-3001-derived ppCO2 limits are time-averaged exposure requirements. Compare only readings averaged over the matching duration; do not apply them to instantaneous values.

measurement_guidance.resting_core_temperature: Measure at consistent times where possible because core temperature has a circadian rhythm. Compare with preflight and personal phase-specific baseline.
measurement_guidance.exercise_core_temperature: Interpret with exercise workload, duration, heart rate, cabin conditions and symptoms.
measurement_guidance.exercise_temperature_rise: The Stahn et al. values are study averages, not operational limits.
measurement_guidance.sampling: Keep resting and exercise measurements separate; do not compare them as if they were the same context.

compound_rules.title: Exercise-associated heat-strain pattern
compound_rules.logic: Elevated exercise core temperature response relative to personal baseline AND elevated resting HR, elevated resting core temp, or active aerobic/resistance workload.
compound_rules.message: A changed exercise core temperature response together with elevated heart rate, resting core temperature, or exercise workload may indicate increased heat strain. This is not a diagnosis of heat illness.
compound_rules.action: Review conditions and trend; escalate if symptomatic or markedly abnormal.
compound_rules.threshold_note: 0.10 C/min ground and 0.15 C/min in-flight are study averages, not medical thresholds.

core_principles: Do not treat missing or stale measurements as normal.
Record timestamp, units, measurement method, mission phase and posture where relevant.
Compare exercise heart rate only at a comparable workload and protocol.
Use the correct averaging window for cabin CO2 limits.
Use personal baselines where no validated NASA numeric reference exists.

reference_audit.purpose: Every existing indicator is explicitly classified for NASA/spaceflight source traceability and numeric-reference availability.
reference_audit.important: A cited study value, cohort average, or operational exercise example is not automatically a universal clinical threshold. Only apply numeric comparisons when the indicator note and original rule specify the correct phase, posture, protocol, and averaging window.

status_legend.nasa_study_association_threshold_not_cli: Study association; not a diagnosis or universal clinical threshold.
status_legend.nasa_cohort_reference_not_universal_limi: Astronaut cohort values; not universal individual limits.
status_legend.nasa_operational_guidance_not_universal_: NASA programme guidance; individual plan takes precedence.
status_legend.no_nasa_reference_found_personal_baselin: No directly applicable NASA reference found; use personal baseline.
status_legend.context_only_no_health_threshold: Context variable; no health alert threshold.
status_legend.user_defined_label_no_nasa_reference: App/input label; not a NASA-defined clinical scale.
